intro: A submerged cathedral takes shape through piano resonance: bare intervals grow into broad chords, then recede. Marcelle Meyer’s 1956 recording makes the distance between the quiet opening and the full keyboard part of the form.
question: How can one piano suggest bells, an organ and distance?

sections.mNote: rising pentatonic figures gain B-major harmony and left-hand triplets

relations.label: The broad melody returns as an echo
relations.basis: Debussy recalls the broad chordal melody in the quieter, lower-register echo section. The matched excerpts lie within the first chordal statement and the echo marked near 268 s. CENS diagonal mean 0.908, sustained 12.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 141.5 s (cache/form/debussy-cathedrale-engloutie.txt, candidate 3; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Fifths before full chords
cues.text: The opening uses bare fifths rather than immediately fixing a major or minor chord. Listen to the space between the rising groups of notes: the piano’s resonance continues where the fingers are no longer making new attacks.
cues.evidence: The score begins with parallel fifths. The report shows a quiet, sparsely attacked opening; it does not align individual intervals to seconds.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The drowned city of Ys
cues.text: The title refers to the Breton legend of Ys, a city swallowed by the sea. The story associated with the prelude describes a submerged cathedral whose bells, chants and organ can still be heard. These are legendary images, not sounds added to the recording.
cues.evidence: The legend and its association with the prelude are documented in the work account linked above: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_cath%C3%A9drale_engloutie

cues.title: Emerging from the mist
cues.text: Through the first expansion, the music becomes more continuous and gains weight. Debussy writes “Peu à peu sortant de la brume” — gradually emerging from the mist. Register, rhythm and chord spacing supply the change without adding another instrument.
cues.evidence: The score places this instruction in the first expansion. Measured changes around 1:14–1:28 and a rising level through 1:40 support its approximate location.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A melody made of chords
cues.text: In the broad chordal passages, follow the top of each chord while also attending to the notes moving beneath it. Parallel motion gives the melodic line thickness rather than merely placing a tune above accompaniment.
cues.evidence: Parallel chord writing is a score feature. The report shows a sustained higher-level span around 1:50–2:40, but does not identify the individual chords.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: An organ without pipes
cues.text: The broad chords suggest an organ, but the piano cannot sustain them indefinitely. Listen to each attack and its decay. Debussy asks for “Sonore sans dureté” — sonorous without harshness — in the principal chordal statement.
cues.evidence: The marking belongs to the score’s principal chordal passage. The sustained higher relative level around 2:00–2:40 suggests this placement, without a bar-level alignment.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Training at the Conservatoire
cues.text: Debussy entered the Paris Conservatoire at ten, studied piano with Marmontel and composition with Guiraud, and won the Prix de Rome in 1884.
cues.evidence: IRCAM’s Debussy biography documents his training and the prize: https://brahms.ircam.fr/fr/composer/claude-debussy/biography

cues.title: A second rise
cues.text: After the quieter withdrawal, another expansion gathers weight. Compare its shorter rise and retreat with the broader chordal span earlier in the piece.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises from the quiet span around 3:00–3:10 to a peak around 3:55, then falls markedly by 4:05. This is a measured contour, not a precisely timed score event.

cues.title: The phrase as an echo
cues.text: Near the end, the broad melody returns more quietly and lower in the keyboard. Debussy explicitly calls it an echo of the earlier phrase; compare the changed texture with the first statement.
cues.evidence: The score marks the later return as an echo. The quieter span around 4:30–4:55 is compatible with that placement; its starting bar has not been aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The title comes afterwards
cues.text: In the printed Préludes, Debussy places each title after its piece, in parentheses. A reader following the score from the start encounters the musical notation before the named image.
cues.evidence: The title placement is visible in the published score and described in this work account: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_cath%C3%A9drale_engloutie

cues.title: Let the resonance finish
cues.text: In the closing passage, let the piano’s remaining resonance complete the phrase. The final attack and the disappearance of the sound are different parts of the ending.
cues.evidence: The report shows a sustained fall in relative level around 5:20–5:35, with no detected new attacks in its final two windows. It does not locate a precise pedal release.

transitions.title: A bass semitone starts the emergence
transitions.how: The opening’s rising fifths return over C in the bass before Debussy lowers that foundation to B and establishes B major. The upper chords preserve the rising pentatonic shape, while left-hand triplets introduce motion beneath them. This is a change of harmonic ground and rhythmic layer, not the arrival of an unrelated tune. The instruction to emerge gradually is realised by adding continuity below a recognisable outline.
transitions.evidence: The Emerging boundary is 1:14, a strong novelty peak; the report shows rising relative level through 1:40. The score’s bass C–B, B-major pentatonic material and left-hand triplets are described in the bar 14–19 analysis at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_cath%C3%A9drale_engloutie. Bar numbers are structural references, not aligned timestamps.

transitions.title: Moving harmony becomes an organ pedal
transitions.how: The rising material passes from B major to E♭ major, then gathers around G dominant-seventh harmony before the broad C-major statement. The left hand exchanges its moving triplets for the weight of a low C foundation, while both hands thicken the melody into parallel chords. The dominant preparation gives the arrival direction; the sustained tonic bass lets the chords above move like a melody rather than a succession of separate cadences.
transitions.evidence: The broad-span boundary is 1:46, a novelty peak following the build around 1:30–1:40. The B-major–E♭-major route, G7 preparation and C-major chordal theme are score features in bars 16–28, summarised at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_cath%C3%A9drale_engloutie. The wider span avoids presenting the approximate map boundary as the exact C-major attack.

transitions.title: The broad chords leave an older fragment
transitions.how: The C-major chordal proclamation thins and sinks in level before C♯-minor material takes over. This quieter idea has already appeared inside the opening: Debussy retrieves a fragment instead of inventing a contrasting song. The bass no longer pins a broad C-major statement in place; changed harmony and a more exposed melodic line make room for a second accumulation. The tonal centre shifts by a semitone, but the returning contour keeps the new passage connected to the first.
transitions.evidence: The Second ascent boundary is 3:04, a novelty peak within the quiet 2:55–3:10 span. The score’s transition at bars 42–46 and C♯-minor recall at bar 47 establish the harmony and thematic link; the report’s competing local key labels are not adopted as score facts.

transitions.title: The chordal melody returns beneath the surface
transitions.how: After the second crest, parallel dominant-seventh chords descend through a withdrawal. Their shared chord shape carries the motion; each is not required to resolve to its own tonic. Debussy then restores the C-major chordal melody quietly, lower on the keyboard and above an oscillating bass figure. The tune survives, but its attack, register and foundation have changed. What previously sounded like a broad proclamation is explicitly marked as an echo.
transitions.evidence: The Distant echo boundary is 4:28, with nearby novelty at 4:32 and quieter levels after 4:00. The score supplies the planed seventh chords and lower C-major echo. The relations file matches 139–151.5 s with 280.5–293 s; that supports the returning melody, not an exact first bar or a machine-detected register.

transitions.title: The echo sheds its accompaniment
transitions.how: The low chordal echo gives way to the opening’s rising pentatonic figures. Debussy removes the oscillating accompaniment and exposes spaced attacks and their resonance again, now within the home C-major field. The final harmony retains D alongside the C-major triad: the added second is allowed to ring rather than being treated as a dissonance that must resolve. The closing link therefore restores the opening’s texture without restoring its tonal uncertainty.
transitions.evidence: The Closing bells boundary is 5:05; the report shows sparse attacks around 5:00 and a sustained decline towards the final decay. The opening-figure recall and final C-major harmony with added D are written features of bars 84–89. The passage timing does not locate a pedal change.

composer.background:
Debussy was born above his parents’ china shop in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, outside Paris. Neither parent was a professional musician. His father’s involvement in the Paris Commune brought imprisonment in 1871; through a connection made during that imprisonment, the boy came to the piano teacher Antoinette Mauté, Verlaine’s mother-in-law. He entered the Paris Conservatoire in 1872, aged ten. Antoine Marmontel trained him as a pianist; Ernest Guiraud later taught him composition. His resistance to harmonic rules developed inside this education: he could play, analyse and compete successfully in the system he came to distrust.

From 1880 he spent summers working for Nadezhda von Meck, Tchaikovsky’s patron, playing chamber music and teaching her children. Travel with her household took him to Italy and Russia. In Paris he accompanied the soprano Marie Vasnier, with whom he had an affair, and wrote songs for her flexible high voice. In their accompaniments, the piano’s register, resonance and passing harmonic changes can supply a second interpretation of the words. The early songs also show how thoroughly he knew the French vocal tradition he would alter.
composer.epithet: He made a chord’s spacing, a scale’s missing notes and an instrument’s register determine the course of a piece.
